[h1]What Orwell is[/h1]

This is likely the first thing you might ask yourself if you're considering buying this game. Basically Orwell is a visual novel. The main way the game communicates is through text and the way you progress the story is by character dialogue. The way you trigger the dialogue is the unusual part. Basically you're a government employee whose job is to spy on people and while you do it by reading their e-mails, browsing their facebook page you're highlighted info you might want to add to the government's archive and investigate it. 

[h1]The Good[/h1]

The way the characters unfold is pulled off incredibly well. Despite me being quite the cynical person the game affected me too when I learned about the people's secrets and their motivations behind their actions. I'm being purposefully vague as I don't want to spoil anything. The art style is also quite unique, albeit it's explained poorly (viewing the world through chunks of data and all that). Another plus is that the game is all text so you could run it on anything. I'm sure an android port would be a piece of cake, and you could also play it on your grandma's chromebook.

[h1]The not-so-good[/h1]

The budget constraints were clear as day to me. The phone calls were all text so they weren't any different from the chat conversations, which broke immersion to me. Some voice acting would have elevated things a lot. Another minus is the way the narrative is presented at times. The character archetypes (hacker, government official, shy girl, punk kid) were really stereotypical and made the otherwise heavy dystopian story feel juvenile and borderline teen comedy-esque. The political commentary seemed really black and white, "good guys vs. bad guys" type of story. All the government officials act incredibly arrogant, almost like cartoon villains and all the civilian characters, as stated above, are just plain archetypes (with a few exceptions). So the game could have done a little better in the writing department.

[h1]The Verdict[/h1]

Orwell is a great visual novel game with a twist, that suffers from a lack of scale (likely due to a limited budget) and some writing flaws, but is overall superb for what it is. Definitely recommended, just don't expect the best game you've ever played.

Orwell belongs in that catagory of indie games which mostly go under the radar due to looking somewhat innocuous and modest, but turn out to be absolutely fantastical and mind blowing upon investigation.

I loved it. It was well written, engaging and interestingly presented. It's full of choice and consequence and has a strong narrative reflecting the ongoing modern debate regarding the paradox of our unlimited freedom of information in the digital age and how that could be used (maliciously or otherwise) to inhibit our personal freedom.

Check it out!

I've been wanting to write a short but to the point review for this game. Mostly because I rarely finish any games in one go. 

Orwell is [b]NOT[/b] going to WOW you. It's not mindblowing, mind you. It will, however, keep you intrigued once you decide to give it a try. 

[u]What's it about?[/u]

It's heavily influenced by the reveals of Edward Snowden. It's about working in the NSA and uncovering personal data in order to get to the truth. It's about whether or not as people we'd sacrifice our "freedom" or our "safety". Overall, an interesting premise.

[u]Right. It's a game, so what's the gameplay like?[/u]

The "game" consists of reading a lot of text and putting certain bits of it together in order to progress to the next chapters. It doesn't sound too engaging but once you start reading through it, it is able to drag you into its universe. There are multiple endings and choices where you need to choose what to reveal for the people you gather information yourself. 

[u]Multiple choices. Does that mean there's a lot of replayability?[/u]

Well, once you get to the conclusion, you sort of feel fulfilled, hence why many of the reviewers of this game have a few hours of gametime. [b]BUT[/b] I think you can easily play the game a second time to do a few things differently. There is some replayability potential.

Good soundtrack, interesting premise, amusing characters, nice artstyle, engaging storyline. I strongly recommend this game if you want something different.

As the term "Orwellian" has made its way into colloquial language - and has, alas, become more widespread in its use as of late - choosing this name alone builds up quite a lot of expectations, and I found those of mine fulfilled. I rever 1984 as one of the greatest books of the 20th century, and in our turbulent days, examining the topic of state-ordered surveillance, it has never lost its edge. While I wouldn't call this game a spiritual successor of the book, it splendidly represents the ideas of Orwell, and even has a few clever references to him sprinkled here and there.

Without spoiling too much of the story, you are a hired investigator examining the online records and phone calls of certain suspicious subjects. What is surprising that in a game about surveillance and suppression, you are given a surprising amount of choice: Whenever conflicting informations emerge, you have to make a choice which one to forward to your superior, and thus influencing their view on the subjects, making them appear as law-abiding citizens or subversive terrorists. This may decide over their life and death, and those of many innocents.

As you close in on the center of a supposed cell of rebellion, you are even presented with a choice concerning your own fate: Will you persevere your original task and rout the suspects, or will you rise against your superiors and the blatant injustice of the system? It all depends on your ability to copy and paste text snippets.
A creepy look into what could be the future very soon. Great game.

I played through this game on Origin and recently received the game through steam via a Humble Monthly Bundle; so I felt it was time to put my thoughts on the game out there. I'm someone who is very aware of the constant privacy invasions of our internet connected lives, and how we are losing ground constantly. One of my favorite books is 1984 by George Orwell, so the name of this game was the first thing to pique my interest before I knew what it was about. Without any major spoilers, you play as an employee of a Big Brother-like watch system over the people in your country at the beginning of its implementation. You spend the game looking at a computer OS style UI where you scan through documents, web pages, and other online material to profile people for this "all-seeing" system. 
     
     The most interesting thing about this game is how well it presents all the different types of dangers (as well as pros if you look for them) with surveillance systems like the United States NSA stuff that has come out over the past years. It does such a good job at it because you aren't just looking at leaked documents about the system, but you ARE the system. Which means you make mistakes (or not) which leads to incorrect profiles and taking things out of context, which  endangers everyone. 

     Orwell is by far the best way to have someone that doesn't understand why national surveillance is bad for its citizens, truly understand all the intricacies and nuances of such a complex issue. I highly reccomend everyone play through this game. I honestly wish everyone had to play through this game so that misinformation and ignorance surrounding this issue would be minimized and we could all work together for the benefit of society as a whole. Play this game, and get someone else to play it; you won't be disappointed!

With "Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" Osmotic Studios and publisher Daedalic Entertainment deliver a narrative surveillance thriller that quietly turns its own core theme into self parody. The player is asked to watch over the privacy of others, while in the background a telemetry chain made of Steam, Unity and Mailchimp wakes up, of which not a single word can be found on the product page.

[h1]What does the product do?[/h1]On first launch the game already talks to Steam, fetches the SDR config for AppID 491950. In parallel Unity reaches out to Google Cloud, generates a persistent userid and ships a full hardware profile. Only after all of this does the player see a brief in game pointer to an external privacy notice.

[h1]Who operates the product?[/h1]Osmotic Studios GmbH (formerly Fellow Traveller)
Daedalic Entertainment GmbH (current publisher)

[h1]Which service providers are involved?[/h1]Osmotic Studios GmbH
Daedalic Entertainment GmbH
Valve Corporation
Unity Technologies
Google, LLC (infrastructure for Unity)
Intuit Mailchimp (owned by Intuit Inc.)
[noparse]Amazon.com, Inc.[/noparse]

[h1]What data is collected?[/h1]
Unique identifiers have been redacted for the review.
[b]Unity Analytics (no visible notice)[/b]
Unity 6000.3.8f1 fires POST requests to the Unity Analytics config and event endpoints. The endpoints resolve to Google Cloud in the United States.
[list][*] Persistent userid and deviceid, sessionid, session_count
[*] appid and build_guid
[*] Full hardware profile: CPU, RAM, VRAM, GPU vendor, driver, D3D12 feature level
[*] OS version, language, mainboard model, machine hostname
[*] Events appStart, appStop, SubsystemInfo, shaderRuntimeInfo
[/list]No OptIn is shown, tracking cannot be turned off inside the game.

[b]Steam Datagram Relay[/b]
The client fetches the Steam SDR configuration for the game and then opens 34 UDP connections to Frankfurt, Stockholm, London, Paris, Vienna, Warsaw, Amsterdam, New York, Chicago, Atlanta, Dallas, Los Angeles, Seattle, Sao Paulo, Buenos Aires, Santiago, Hong Kong, Tokyo, Seoul, Singapore, Mumbai, Sydney, Johannesburg and Dubai. For a pure single player thriller this fanout provides no benefit.

[b]Mailchimp newsletter[/b]
The in game newsletter sends first name, email and the tag "Orwell" straight to the Mailchimp REST API. The client uses a fixed HTTP Basic Auth credential baked into the build, "user:[redacted]-us14", which is a full Mailchimp API key visible in any network capture. The server response leaks list metadata, sender, statistics and a contact address (Papenstrasse 27, 22089 Hamburg) that differs from the one in the privacy notice. Headers reveal hosting in AWS us east 2.

[h1]GDPR violations in detail[/h1]
[b]Unity Analytics without consent[/b]
[list][*] Art. 5(1)a Transparency: Transmission starts before the user is informed
[*] Art. 6 Lawfulness: No consent, no documented legitimate interest
[*] Art. 7 Consent: No OptIn dialog, the pointer arrives too late
[*] Art. 13 Information obligation: Unity Analytics and Google Cloud are not named
[*] Art. 25 Privacy by Design: Tracking is default, no in game switch
[*] Art. 44ff Third country transfer: US Google Cloud, no SCC notice in game
[/list]
[b]Mailchimp newsletter[/b]
[list][*] Art. 5(1)f Integrity: The API key sits in plain text in the game binary
[*] Art. 13: Hosting in the US is not disclosed in game
[*] Art. 25: No server side email validation
[*] Art. 44ff: Third country transfer to the US, no visible safeguard
[/list]
[b]Steam SDR[/b]
Art. 5(1)c Data minimization: 34 worldwide relays for a solo title are excessive.

[h1]Privacy policy and Opt-in/Opt-out[/h1]
The Steam product page does not show or link any privacy policy or EULA. Inside the game a short pointer appears during profile creation, but only after Steam SDR and Unity have already shipped data abroad. The Steam age rating in Germany is "12 and up" while the Osmotic privacy notice itself requires a minimum age of 18. No age verification takes place.

A second oversight: the in game privacy notice is supposed to exist in English and German. In reality the "German" file is a word for word copy of the English text, only the headline reads "Datenschutzerklärung". A German speaking user has no proper localized notice available in game, which under Art. 12 GDPR is a serious flaw.

The notice itself does not name Unity Analytics, does not mention the Google Cloud infrastructure, does not list the Mailchimp pipeline and says nothing about a hardcoded API key inside the client.

[h1]Can this behavior be blocked?[/h1]
Yes, largely. The Unity Analytics endpoints, the Mailchimp REST API and the Steam SDR config request can all be blocked at the network layer without breaking gameplay. "Orwell" is a pure single player title, neither Unity Analytics nor SDR are required for it to run.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]"Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You" stages a surveillance state and trains the player to quietly oversee the data of strangers, while at the same time keeping a close eye inside its own engine room.

The Steam product page skips any data protection or EULA information, the in game pointer arrives too late and in a language version that is German only by name. Unity Analytics runs without a visible OptIn through Google Cloud in the United States, the newsletter pipeline goes through Mailchimp with an API key baked into the client, and Steam SDR opens 34 UDP connections worldwide for a solo title.

The thematic punch line lands twice here, once in the script and once in the network log.

[h1]Additional Info[/h1]
Additional details, including a full connection overview for blocking access, involved IPv4 addresses, company information and the German version of the review, are available as usual at [url=https://gameindustry.eu]GameIndustry[/url]. If you're interested, join the [url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/penguindome]Penguin Domination[/url] group to stay informed about new reviews on Steam.

It's hard to say that either Orwell's story or its interface is earth-shattering in any way, but put together they create an experience that's enough to keep you always running after what's around the next corner. As on-the-nose as it may be to call your game on state surveillance "Orwell", the narrative inside is more restrained and explores accurate and disturbing tactics used by state spies. You get the sense that the "choice" in the story is often somewhat an illusion, but maybe that's the point. It's a game that empowers you by letting you crawl inside peoples' PCs and phones while teaching you about privacy invasion and only once it's put you through the preset experiences it thinks are necessary does it let you decide what to do about this spy apparatus.

I don't think anything could have prepared me for Orwell.

Playing the role of a law enforcement agent, researching a potential terrorist cell through the social media and communications of its members, the simple browser-styled interface makes it easy to lose yourself in the characters, their interactions and the over-arching story which often hits close-to-home in 2017.

Overall, a really relaxing play and an interesting look at real-life issues surrounding privacy, social media and free speech.

This game was surprisingly effective. I went in expecting some heavy-handed story based purely on the title, but apart from some suspension of disbelief problems I really enjoyed the game. The UI was a masterpiece, the story interesting enough, but it's the characters where Orwell really shines. Each and every one of them felt believable and real, and I, at least, ended up rather moved by some of the characters and their motivations.

What I thought was especially interesting was how they're written to be very open to interpetation and to your preconception. The user-selectable portraits really help in this regard, as they each seem to represent different facets of the cast's personalities. A novel approach to interactive fiction, and I highly recommend it.

If you read 1984, this is exactly what you'd expect: you're big brother. You're going to need to do some soul-searching after this. And you're going to need to play it more than once.

Here's what happens: You get told to look up this woman who may have commited a crime. You don't actually look up anything, you just click on the page it gives you. It highlights what in that page you are supposed to save. It tells you when you have collected all of the information from that page and moves on to the next one. The entire game is just looking at these pages, or conversations, and dragging highlighted text or photos to a folder. That's it.
This game doesn't require thinking, not really. I thought the fact that you could choose what text you send over meant you could omit anything you wanted, but then it won't move on to the next series of pages. You have to send it something, and it pretty much all leads to the same outcomes.
It could have been a lot better. If it wasn't so linear, if you were left to search and find things on your own, if you could pick out which people to build a dossier on, anything like that would have made this awesome.

As the name says, this game is highly inspired by George Orwell's works, specifically "1984", and depicts a very plausible scenario for the near-future. Is it dystopian? Not sure, since it feels so close to home.
The fact is, it is a great and new way to the narrative genre. In a investigation genre, you are the anti-ethical birdwatcher, except you are not watching birds, but possible "terrorists". Who is to blame? Who is the guilty? Does it really matter?
I can't wait for more games following this lead (pun-intended), and couldn't recommend more for anyone interested in Unique games!

Orwell is one of those incredibly rare games that suck you into the story within minutes - and you stay glued to your screen until the game finishes.
It's narrative is complex and it becomes incredibly easy to believe that you are an agent working with the Orwell Surveillance Program. The choices you have to make have lasting concequences - both good and bad, and the ending depends entirely on the way you have played the game. It also works well in that you have to play the game multiple times to discover all choices and endings; it is often fun to go back and make the decisions you strayed from previously and seeing their impact on the progression of the narrative.
If you want a game with impact that has a simple premise, but delves into a web of interlinking plotlines and characters, then this is the game for you.
I, for one, cannot wait for the second season to be out; it cannot come soon enough!
One of the best games I've ever played. I think I need to say no more?

This game worked perfectly for me and to quickly point out the main reasons why people could like or dislike it, here I go:

- Story is quite brief.
- It doesn't bother with advanced visuals and sophisticated soundtrack.
- You will have to read stuff to play it.
- The premises are absolutely nothing new to the world of conspiracy theories.

Now in a little more detail and opinion:

[h1]Brief story[/h1]

The game doesn't take too much time to complete and although in the end it really doesn't matter what you choose (duh) it still might keep you wondering what could go differently. Because it does offer more than one chance to actually affect the progress.

Still, the game might feel like it's taking a while because at some points you may find yourself struggling to find that one crucial piece that's needed to go forward, at others - you will get overwhelmed by the amount of choice. Not that it's bad, but if you're not really patient you might get actually bored.

[h1]No pretence[/h1]

The game really doesn't bother to give you some superb visuals and sounds. But the fact is it doesn't really need those. I don't even know if the voice-over of some parts of the game would be appropriate or not. But "Orwell" does have a distinct style to it which actually brings some of it's own atmosphere along without a claim to be something very special.

What is special though is an attempt to create an intertwined character development (not for you personally, sorry) that can keep you willing to go on and complete the whole story.

[h1]Reading[/h1]

Well, this game is 90% text. Please read it, please read it carefully and not just because the game plot demands it but because every piece of information in this game can be actually useful later on or right now or maybe a couple of minutes before you made that decision you now regret.

[h1]Conspiracy theories[/h1]

This game is called "Orwell" for an obvious reason. It doesn't even need an explanation. Like the setting? Fancy the idea of total government (or other type of) control? Or maybe you're completely against it? Well, in any case, the game gives some food for thought if you haven't yet though about this topic that much or explores those scenarios you might've already seen somewhere, but this time with you behind the wheel... or rather exactly not behind the wheel (duh).


[h1]Overall opinion[/h1]

This is not the best game of all ages, but I believe its creators brought exactly what they've wanted to bring into it. Which means "Orwell" serves its purpose perfectly.

I would recommend it for anyone who likes smart and level entertainment and doesn't mind spending some time exploring the world of text rather than beautifully rendered landscapes.

I'm going to get straight to the point with this review. This is one of my favorite games of all time. Period. It is a wonderfully written, powerful games that forces you to come to terms with your personal beleifs. It's as much an exercise in 
self-exploration as it is in game design. Speaking of game design, this is one of the most slickly designed games ever, I never ran into any glitch or other imperfection. Also, if you are worried that it might not feel like your choices matter, I'll put that to rest, I don't want to spoil some of the great moments this game has, so I won't give examples, but there are many times in this game where your choices really feel alive and impactful.
